analysis.one_liner: Bars the largest online platforms from favoring their own products over competitors using their platforms.
analysis.headline: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved it with bipartisan support in early 2022 and placed it on the Senate calendar, but it never received a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it unlawful for very large online platforms to favor their own products over competitors on the platform, use nonpublic data gathered from business users to build competing products, block rivals from interoperating with the platform, or prevent users from uninstalling preinstalled apps. It applies to platforms with 50 million or more U.S. monthly users owned by a company with over $550 billion in U.S. sales or market capitalization, with an alternative test for privately held companies. The Federal Trade Commission and Justice Department would enforce it, with civil penalties of up to 15 percent of U.S. revenue and, for repeat offenders, possible forfeiture of executive pay.
analysis.who_benefits: Small businesses, app developers, and other companies that sell through dominant platforms, plus the consumers who buy from them. The bill would require platforms to treat these business users the same as the platform's own products, open the platform to rival services, and let users uninstall preinstalled apps or change default settings.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Small sellers, app developers, and platform users

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits covered platforms from favoring their own products, services, or lines of business over competing business users in ways that materially harm competition.
Bans platforms from using nonpublic data generated by business users to offer their own competing products, and from blocking business users from taking their own data to other systems.

Requires platforms to allow competitors to interoperate with the same platform features available to the platform's own products, and stops steering users by preventing them from uninstalling preinstalled apps or changing default settings.

Enforced by the FTC, the Justice Department, and state attorneys general, with civil penalties up to 15 percent of U.S. revenue for the period of violation and possible executive compensation forfeiture for repeat offenders.

analysis.who_pays: The large platform operators, which would face new restrictions on how they run their marketplaces, app stores, and operating systems, plus civil penalties and possible executive pay forfeiture for violations. Some costs could be passed to users through changes to services like bundled free shipping or preinstalled features.
analysis.who_pays_short: Amazon, Apple, Google, and similar platforms

drawbacks.text: Platforms argued the rules would force them to remove useful features and integrations and could weaken privacy and security; the bill's affirmative defenses let operators justify conduct that is necessary for safety, privacy, security, or core functionality, but critics warned that the line between illegal self-preferencing and ordinary product design would be litigated for years.

The covered-platform tests are keyed to being publicly traded and to market-capitalization, sales, or EBITDA thresholds above $550 billion or $30 billion; opponents argued this design regulates a named set of U.S. companies rather than defining conduct, and that foreign-owned apps popular with American users could sit outside the rules.
Because the bill was never debated on the floor, none of these design questions got a public test through amendments or a vote.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is concrete: businesses that depend on dominant platforms would compete on closer to equal terms, and users would have more choice over preinstalled software and defaults. The costs are real but bounded — compliance burdens on the platforms and genuine uncertainty about where the line falls — and the bill tried to address the worst objections with affirmative defenses for security, privacy, and core functionality. The stronger objection is not the design but the outcome: it never received a floor debate or vote, so neither the benefits nor the acknowledged risks were ever tested.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved it in January 2022 and it was placed on the Senate calendar in March 2022, but it sat there for ten months without the Majority Leader ever bringing it to the floor, and the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Amy Klobuchar introduced the bill on October 18, 2021 with a bipartisan group of original cosponsors including Republicans Chuck Grassley, John Kennedy, Cynthia Lummis, Lindsey Graham, and Josh Hawley alongside Democrats Dick Durbin, Richard Blumenthal, Cory Booker, Mazie Hirono, and Mark Warner.
The Senate Judiciary Committee ordered the bill reported favorably with a substitute amendment on January 20, 2022.

The committee, chaired for this purpose by Sen. Durbin, formally reported the bill on March 2, 2022, and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 301 — a step that made it eligible for floor action but guaranteed nothing.
No further action was taken for the rest of the Congress; the bill never received a floor debate or vote, and the Congress ended January 3, 2023.

The bill faced an intense public campaign from the major platforms it would regulate — Amazon, Apple, Google, and Meta — which spent heavily on lobbying and advertising warning that the rules would break popular products and favor foreign competitors; the Senate Majority Leader, Chuck Schumer, never scheduled it for a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large online platforms that the bill would have regulated are better off: their rules for self-preferencing, use of business-user data, and control of app stores and operating systems remain unchanged. Small businesses and consumers did not receive the protections the bill offered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The platforms it would have regulated

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.role: U.S. Senator from Minnesota, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led the effort to advance it through the Senate Judiciary Committee.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.role: U.S. Senator from Iowa, lead Republican cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Joined as the lead Republican cosponsor, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship.

for.name: Sen. Dick Durbin
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill out of committee with a substitute amendment on March 2, 2022.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate floor vote after it was placed on the calendar in March 2022.

against.name: Amazon, Apple, Google, and Meta
against.role: The large online platforms the bill would cover
against.what_they_did: Ran a sustained lobbying and public-relations campaign against the bill, spending heavily on lobbying and ads warning it would harm popular products and help foreign competitors.

against.name: Tech industry trade groups
against.what_they_did: Organized opposition, arguing the bill would degrade products, harm small businesses, and advantage foreign rivals.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was unusual for its bipartisan sponsorship — a Democrat leading with the top Republican on antitrust, and cosponsors split 7 Democrats and 6 Republicans — and it cleared the Judiciary Committee on a bipartisan basis; it never reached a floor vote where party positions would have been counted.

industries.industry: Large online platforms (Amazon, Apple, Google, Meta)
industries.note: The bill would bar them from self-preferencing, using business-user data to build competing products, restricting interoperability, or blocking app uninstalls, with penalties up to 15 percent of U.S. revenue. Their interest in blocking the bill ran against the small sellers and consumers the rules were designed to protect.

industries.industry: Small businesses and app developers selling through dominant platforms
industries.note: They would compete on closer to equal terms with the platform's own products, gain data portability and interoperability rights, and be protected from retaliation for reporting violations.

Restrictions on self-preferencing and data use would open parts of these markets to rivals, but platforms could also no longer use some integration practices that today bundle advertising and distribution at no visible charge to users.
